newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end higher,CPI sparks short-covering.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end higher,CPI sparks short-covering.

text.p: Sparked by a report of benign inflation at the retail level, U.S. Treasuries rose sharply on Tuesday.
But the gains, attributed largely to short-covering, took place in the first hour of trading, with Treasuries sticking to very tight ranges the rest of the day.
Late Tuesday, the 30-year bond was at 94-8/32, up 30/32 from Monday. Its yield fell to 7.09 percent from 7.17 percent.
Demand was highest in the 10-year note, which rose 23/32 and dropped in yield to 6.87 percent from 6.98 percent.
Traders said the rally was purely technical in nature, as dealers were forced to cover short positions after the Consumer Price Index (CPI) came in below expectations.
"People were short and bearish for a while. This is just a little recovery," said Tom Macirowski, senior Treasury strategist at Goldman Sachs & Co.

The Labor Department reported that the CPI increased 0.1 percent in March, while the CPI excluding food and energy rose 0.2 percent -- below expectations of 0.2 percent and 0.3 percent rises, respectively.
Treasury prices jumped on the data, with the long bond up as much as 1-1/4 points, before giving back some of those gains.
The rally was led by the longer end, which players said indicated the market had not changed sentiment on Federal Reserve policy, despite the big drop in yields.

"Nobody feels this data eliminates the prospects of addtional (Fed) restraint," said William Sullivan, director of money markets research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. "But no doubt the CPI was beneficial to the back end because (low inflation) reduces nominal yields."
The lack of follow-through buying after the data signaled that the market remains bearish, players said.

"We are another (strong) economic report away from 7.25 percent" on the 30-year bond, said Joe LaVorgna, financial market economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "CPI shouldn't change the call on the Fed ... There's still much data between now and the May (Fed) meeting."
Helping the market on Tuesday was a 135-point gain in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, and, to a lesser extent, declines in commodities prices -- mainly gold.
The strong CPI caught many players off guard, as dealers had braced for a strong report, adding to the short positions taken on in recent sessions.
Consequently, those shorts had to be covered. Indeed, activity was very heavy in the first hour after the report, with volume at $16 billion from 0830 EDT to 0930 EDT, according to GovPX.
For the day as a whole, volume was about $88 billion -- 17 percent above an average Tuesday in the second quarter and 11 percent above the average of the past three CPI releases.
Goldman's Macirowski noted that the market should remain under pressure for the time being given a string of potentially strong economic news upcoming and next week's two- and five-year note auction.
"There's a whole lot of news to get through until people change their (Fed) view substantially," he said.
On Wednesday, March housing starts are due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, followed at 0915 EDT/1315 GMT by the Fed's industrial production/capacity utilization report.
Traders noted that any gains in the market are capped by the inability to breach 107-28 on the June boind contract. "It's been a brick wall," said one head trader at a large U.S. bank.
He said that should the 108 level be breached, then the market might be able to rally more, but that does not seem very likely.
"We are still a little bearish," he said. "I would sell again. And I would look for the Fed (rate hike) view to reassert itself."
The market on Tuesday shrugged off a 0.6 percent gain in the Redbook Reserach weekly retail sales index and a 0.3 percent increase in business inventories in January.

Meanwhile, the two-year note was at 99-21/32, up 5/32, with its yield falling to 6.44 percent from 6.53 percent. The three-year note closed up 8/32 at 98-5/32, yielding 6.60 percent. The five-year note traded up 13/32 at 99-14/32 to yield 6.76 percent.

The three-month bill ended the day down one basis point at at 5.15 percent, while the six-month bill was down four basis points at 5.40 percent. The year-bill was at 5.63 percent, down six basis points.
